subChunks.title: Tables — The Shape of Recorded Knowledge
subChunks.hookHtml: Every record the Academy has ever kept — every apprentice, every quest, every grade — sits in a table. Before you write a single query, you must learn to read a table. The shape of the data dictates the shape of the question you can ask.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What a table is

A table is a grid. Rows are records, columns are attributes. A table named apprentices might look like this:

id  | name      | rank        | xp
----+-----------+-------------+------
 1  | Alice     | Apprentice  | 1200
 2  | Bjorn     | Adept       | 2400
 3  | Cassia    | Mage        | 4800
 4  | Dorian    | Novice      |   80

Four rows. Four columns. Each column has a type — id and xp are integers, name and rank are text. The combination of column names + types is the table's schema.

Why this matters

SQL doesn't ask "give me Alice's XP." It asks "give me the xp column from the apprentices row where name = 'Alice'." The query is shaped by the schema. Wrong column name → query fails. Wrong type comparison → query fails or returns garbage. Reading the schema is the first move every time.

The vocabulary

  • Database — a collection of tables (e.g. "academy_db")
  • Table — a named grid of rows and columns (e.g. "apprentices")
  • Row (or record, or tuple) — one entity stored in the table
  • Column (or field, or attribute) — one named piece of information per row
  • Primary key — a column whose value uniquely identifies each row (almost always id)
  • NULL — the absence of a value. Different from 0 or empty string. We'll meet NULL properly in sql-b.

Reading a schema fluently

When you see this:

quests(id INT PRIMARY KEY,
       title TEXT NOT NULL,
       xp INT NOT NULL,
       difficulty TEXT,
       completed_by INT)

You should immediately think: "a quest has an id, a title, an XP value, an optional difficulty, and an optional reference to who completed it. Title and xp are required; difficulty and completed_by may be null." That instinct is the foundation of every query you'll ever write.

storyBeats.text: You descend a long stone staircase into the Academy's Hall of Records. The air is cool and dry. Shelves stretch into the dim distance, each one packed with leather-bound ledgers. A figure in deep blue robes glances up from an enormous open volume.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Welcome, apprentice. Down here we keep everything. Every name, every grade, every quest ever undertaken. Other apprentices come asking me questions — "who has the highest XP?", "how many novices joined last month?" — and I answer them by reading these ledgers. SQL is the language of asking questions of ledgers. But before questions, you must learn to read.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Each ledger is what we call a table. Look — this one is the apprentices ledger. Every row is one apprentice. Every column is one fact about them — their name, their rank, their experience points.

storyBeats.speaker: The apprentices ledger
storyBeats.text:
id  | name      | rank        | xp
----+-----------+-------------+------
 1  | Alice     | Apprentice  | 1200
 2  | Bjorn     | Adept       | 2400
 3  | Cassia    | Mage        | 4800
 4  | Dorian    | Novice      |   80

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Notice the columns have types. The id column holds whole numbers — integers. The name column holds text. If you ask me for the name of apprentice with xp greater than two thousand, I can do that. If you ask me for the name of an apprentice greater than two thousand — that's nonsense. Names aren't numbers. The types tell us which questions are shaped correctly.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Always start by reading the schema. What columns exist? What types? What's the primary key? The schema is the map. Without it, every query is a guess. Now study the example ledger below — and then I'll teach you to ask your first question.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Read the schema

Before we run a single query, study the schema below. Identify:

  • Which columns are required (NOT NULL)
  • Which columns are the primary key
  • What type each column holds
  • What questions you could not meaningfully ask of this table (e.g. "name > 100")

Then continue to the retrieval check — we'll test whether you've internalised the shape.
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
-- The 'apprentices' table schema
CREATE TABLE apprentices (
  id   INT  PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  rank TEXT NOT NULL,
  xp   INT  NOT NULL
);

-- And here is the data inside it:
--
-- id  | name    | rank        | xp
-- ----+---------+-------------+------
--  1  | Alice   | Apprentice  | 1200
--  2  | Bjorn   | Adept       | 2400
--  3  | Cassia  | Mage        | 4800
--  4  | Dorian  | Novice      |   80
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who has never seen a database what a table is and why every column has a type. Use the apprentices table as your example, and explain why "give me apprentices where rank > 100" is a malformed question.

options: One record (one entity) stored in a table
One named attribute that every record shares
A type definition like INT or TEXT
A relationship between two tables
questions.correctAnswer: One record (one entity) stored in a table
questions.explanationHtml: A row is one record — one apprentice, one quest, one event. A column is the named attribute (e.g. xp); a row is one full entity with values for every column.

options: A column whose value uniquely identifies each row
The first column in a table
A column that cannot be NULL
A reserved keyword for sorting
questions.correctAnswer: A column whose value uniquely identifies each row
questions.explanationHtml: The primary key uniquely identifies each row. There can only be one primary-key value per row, and no two rows can share it. Almost always called id.

questions.questionHtml:
Given this schema, which question is type-incorrect — i.e. malformed because it compares mismatched types?

apprentices(id INT, name TEXT, rank TEXT, xp INT)
options: Find apprentices where name = 1200
Find apprentices where xp > 2000
Find apprentices where rank = 'Mage'
Find apprentices where id = 3
questions.explanationHtml: name is TEXT, but 1200 is an integer. The other three compare each column to a value of its declared type. SQL engines will sometimes coerce types implicitly, but this is exactly the kind of bug you should learn to spot in your head before the query runs.

questions.questionHtml: Two friends describe "a database." Whose description is most accurate?
options: "A collection of named tables, where each table holds rows of structured data."
"A single big spreadsheet with every fact in one place."
"A folder of plain text files you grep through."
"A program that writes code automatically based on questions."
questions.correctAnswer: "A collection of named tables, where each table holds rows of structured data."
questions.explanationHtml: A database is a collection of tables. Each table has its own schema, its own rows, its own purpose. The relational model's whole power comes from breaking data into multiple specialised tables and joining them — we'll meet joins later. The other answers describe spreadsheets, file systems, or AI tools — all distinct from a relational database.

subChunks.title: Your First Query — SELECT, FROM, WHERE
subChunks.hookHtml: You can read a ledger. Now you'll question one. The three keywords that do 80% of all SQL work are SELECT, FROM, and WHERE. Master them and you can retrieve any single fact from any table the Academy keeps.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The basic shape of a query

Every read query in SQL has the same skeleton:

SELECT <columns>
FROM <table>
WHERE <condition>;

That's it. Add other clauses later, but this is the spine.

SELECT — choosing columns

-- All columns:
SELECT * FROM apprentices;

-- Specific columns:
SELECT name, xp FROM apprentices;

-- Rename in the result with AS:
SELECT name AS apprentice_name, xp AS experience
FROM apprentices;

* is convenient for exploring; in production code, list columns explicitly so the query doesn't break when someone adds a new column.

FROM — choosing the table

FROM apprentices says "the rows we're working with come from this table." You'll see fancier FROM clauses later (with joins) but for one table, it's just the table name.

WHERE — filtering rows

Without WHERE, the query returns every row. With WHERE, it returns only rows where the condition is true.

-- Apprentices with more than 1000 XP:
SELECT name, xp FROM apprentices
WHERE xp > 1000;

-- A specific name:
SELECT * FROM apprentices
WHERE name = 'Alice';

-- Exact rank:
SELECT name FROM apprentices
WHERE rank = 'Mage';

String literals are single-quoted

Pay attention: 'Alice', not "Alice". Double quotes have a different meaning in standard SQL (they refer to identifiers like column names). Single quotes always mean "this is a string value." Many SQL engines tolerate double quotes for strings, but writing single quotes is the portable habit.

Common comparison operators

OperatorMeaning
=Equal
<> or !=Not equal
< <= > >=Less / less-or-equal / greater / greater-or-equal

Reading queries in your head

Read SQL inside-out, last-clause-first:

SELECT name, xp
FROM apprentices
WHERE rank = 'Mage';

"From the apprentices table, take the rows where rank is Mage. From those rows, give me name and xp." The engine actually executes WHERE before SELECT — filtering happens first, then the chosen columns are projected.

storyBeats.text: Cipher slides the ledger toward you and produces a quill.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Three words. SELECT — the columns you want. FROM — the table they live in. WHERE — the filter that decides which rows. Three words and you can ask almost anything.

storyBeats.speaker: Three forms of the same shape
Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Watch the quotes. 'Mage' is a string — single quotes. Double quotes mean something else entirely in SQL — they refer to identifiers. If you write WHERE rank = "Mage" in a strict engine, it asks "is the value of the column called Mage equal to the value of the column called rank?" — which makes no sense. Single quotes for strings. Always.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: And read the query inside-out. SELECT name, xp FROM apprentices WHERE xp > 1000: start with apprentices. Filter to rows with xp over a thousand. Then project name and xp from each. The clauses appear in one order; the engine evaluates them in another. Knowing that order will save you when queries get complicated.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
🪄 Cast your first query

The Headmaster wants the names and XP of every apprentice with at least 2,000 XP. Write a single SELECT query against the apprentices table that:

  • Returns two columns: name and xp
  • Includes only rows where xp >= 2000
  • You can order them however you like — order isn't tested

The right pane runs your query against a real SQLite database as you type. Submit when the result looks correct.

Reference data (already loaded):

id | name    | rank        | xp
---+---------+-------------+------
 1 | Alice   | Apprentice  | 1200
 2 | Bjorn   | Adept       | 2400
 3 | Cassia  | Mage        | 4800
 4 | Dorian  | Novice      |   80
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
-- Write a query that returns name and xp
-- for apprentices with at least 2000 XP.
SELECT
  -- columns here
FROM apprentices
WHERE
  -- your filter here
;

guidedPracticeTests.label: Returns the right number of rows (2)
guidedPracticeTests.setup: CREATE TABLE apprentices (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, rank TEXT NOT NULL, xp INTEGER NOT NULL); INSERT INTO apprentices VALUES (1,'Alice','Apprentice',1200),(2,'Bjorn','Adept',2400),(3,'Cassia','Mage',4800),(4,'Dorian','Novice',80);

guidedPracticeTests.label: Returns Bjorn and Cassia (any order)
guidedPracticeTests.expectedQuery: SELECT name, xp FROM apprentices WHERE xp >= 2000

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo Challenge — From scratch

Same data, slightly harder ask: write a query that returns the names of apprentices whose rank is not 'Novice' and whose XP is greater than 1,000.

  • Return only the name column
  • Filter by both conditions
  • Three apprentices should match

If you get stuck, peek at the guided practice for the WHERE-clause shape.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: In your own words, explain what SELECT, FROM, and WHERE each do. Then explain why the query SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE rank = "Mage" — note the double quotes — would fail or behave unexpectedly in a strict SQL engine.

questions.questionHtml: In a SQL query, what does the WHERE clause do?
options: Filters rows so only those matching the condition are returned
Picks which columns appear in the result
Sorts the output
Specifies which table to read from
questions.correctAnswer: Filters rows so only those matching the condition are returned
questions.explanationHtml: SELECT chooses columns; FROM chooses the table; WHERE filters which rows. Sorting is done with ORDER BY (next sub-chunk).

questions.questionHtml:
Using the apprentices table from the lesson, what does this query return?

SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE xp >= 2000;
options: Bjorn, Cassia
Alice, Bjorn, Cassia
Cassia
Alice, Bjorn
questions.explanationHtml: Bjorn (xp=2400) and Cassia (xp=4800) both satisfy xp ≥ 2000. Alice (1200) and Dorian (80) don't. Only the name column is selected, so just two names come back.

questions.questionHtml: Which of these queries selects the names of apprentices whose rank is not 'Novice'?
options: SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE rank <> 'Novice';
SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE rank NOT 'Novice';
SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE rank = NOT 'Novice';
SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE rank ~ 'Novice';
questions.correctAnswer: SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE rank <> 'Novice';
questions.explanationHtml: <> (or equivalently !=) means "not equal". The other forms are not valid SQL syntax for inequality.

questions.questionHtml:
Two apprentices write almost the same query. Which subtle difference matters?

-- Apprentice A:
SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE name = 'Alice';

-- Apprentice B:
SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE name = "Alice";
options: Apprentice A is correct; B's double quotes refer to an identifier, not a string, and may fail in strict engines
Both are equivalent — SQL treats single and double quotes identically
Apprentice B is correct; single quotes are for column names
Both are wrong; SQL strings must use backticks
questions.correctAnswer: Apprentice A is correct; B's double quotes refer to an identifier, not a string, and may fail in strict engines
questions.explanationHtml: In standard SQL, single quotes denote string literals; double quotes denote identifiers (table or column names that contain reserved words or special characters). Many engines (MySQL by default) tolerate double-quoted strings, but PostgreSQL and the SQL standard do not. Always single-quote strings — it's the portable habit.

subChunks.title: Ordering and Limiting — ORDER BY, LIMIT
subChunks.hookHtml: SQL doesn't promise to return rows in any particular order. "The top 5 apprentices by XP" only makes sense if you tell SQL sort first, then take 5. ORDER BY and LIMIT are the two clauses that turn an unordered set into a ranked list.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The default order is undefined

This may surprise you: a relational database does not guarantee row order unless you ask. Two engines, or even two runs of the same query on the same data, may return rows in different orders. If you care about order, you must say so.

ORDER BY — sorting the result

-- Lowest XP first (ascending — the default):
SELECT name, xp FROM apprentices
ORDER BY xp;

-- Highest XP first (descending):
SELECT name, xp FROM apprentices
ORDER BY xp DESC;

-- Sort by multiple columns:
SELECT name, rank, xp FROM apprentices
ORDER BY rank, xp DESC;

Multi-column sort goes left-to-right: rows are first sorted by rank; ties on rank are broken by xp DESC.

LIMIT — taking the top N

-- The single highest-XP apprentice:
SELECT name, xp FROM apprentices
ORDER BY xp DESC
LIMIT 1;

-- The top 3:
SELECT name, xp FROM apprentices
ORDER BY xp DESC
LIMIT 3;

LIMIT caps the number of rows returned after ORDER BY runs. Without ORDER BY, "LIMIT 3" gives you three arbitrary rows — almost never what you want.

The full skeleton, expanded

SELECT <columns>
FROM <table>
WHERE <condition>
ORDER BY <columns>
LIMIT <n>;

The clauses always appear in this order, even if you only use some of them. Forget the order, the engine throws a syntax error.

Engine-specific note

LIMIT works in PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, MariaDB. SQL Server uses TOP N directly after SELECT. Oracle (older versions) uses ROWNUM. The standard is FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY, which most modern engines now support. For learning, LIMIT is the friendliest — and what you'll see in 80% of code.

storyBeats.text: Cipher closes the ledger and pulls a different one closer — a thinner volume bound in red.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Now then. The Headmaster sent a runner this morning. He wants the names of the top three apprentices by XP, posted on the Hall board by noon. How do you ask the ledger that?

storyBeats.speaker: You
storyBeats.text: Top three by XP — that's a sort and then a take.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Exactly. ORDER BY xp DESC sorts highest-first. LIMIT 3 takes the first three. Without ordering, the ledger does not promise any particular sequence — "give me three apprentices" might give you any three.

storyBeats.speaker: Top 3 by XP
storyBeats.text:
SELECT name, xp
FROM apprentices
ORDER BY xp DESC
LIMIT 3;

-- Result, given the ledger we have:
-- name    | xp
-- --------+------
-- Cassia  | 4800
-- Bjorn   | 2400
-- Alice   | 1200

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: And remember the order of the clauses. SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT — always in that sequence. Different engines have a couple of variations on LIMIT — SQL Server uses TOP, Oracle has its own form — but PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQLite all use LIMIT, and that's most of what you'll meet.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
🪄 Top of the leaderboard

The Headmaster wants the top 3 apprentices by XP, highest first. Write a single SELECT query that:

  • Returns two columns: name and xp
  • Sorts by xp descending
  • Returns at most 3 rows

Reference data:

id | name    | rank        | xp
---+---------+-------------+------
 1 | Alice   | Apprentice  | 1200
 2 | Bjorn   | Adept       | 2400
 3 | Cassia  | Mage        | 4800
 4 | Dorian  | Novice      |   80
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
-- Top 3 apprentices by XP, highest first.
SELECT name, xp
FROM apprentices
-- ORDER BY ... ?
-- LIMIT ... ?
;

guidedPracticeTests.label: Returns 3 rows
guidedPracticeTests.setup: CREATE TABLE apprentices (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, rank TEXT NOT NULL, xp INTEGER NOT NULL); INSERT INTO apprentices VALUES (1,'Alice','Apprentice',1200),(2,'Bjorn','Adept',2400),(3,'Cassia','Mage',4800),(4,'Dorian','Novice',80);

guidedPracticeTests.label: Cassia, Bjorn, Alice in that exact order (sorted by xp DESC)
guidedPracticeTests.expectedQuery: SELECT name, xp FROM apprentices ORDER BY xp DESC LIMIT 3

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo Challenge — Bottom of the pile

Same data, opposite question: write a query that returns the two apprentices with the lowest XP, lowest first. Return their name and xp.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain why a query with LIMIT but no ORDER BY is almost always wrong. Use the apprentices ledger as your example, and describe what could go wrong if a junior writes "give me 5 apprentices, LIMIT 5" without ordering them.

questions.questionHtml: What does ORDER BY xp do, with no DESC keyword?
options: Sorts ascending — lowest xp first
Sorts descending — highest xp first
Returns rows in whatever order the engine prefers
Throws an error — DESC is required
questions.explanationHtml: Ascending is the default. ORDER BY xp and ORDER BY xp ASC are equivalent. To reverse, write ORDER BY xp DESC.

questions.questionHtml:
What does this query return, given the apprentices table?

SELECT name, xp FROM apprentices
ORDER BY xp DESC
LIMIT 2;
options: Cassia 4800, Bjorn 2400
Dorian 80, Alice 1200
Cassia 4800, Alice 1200
Alice 1200, Bjorn 2400
questions.explanationHtml: Sort by xp descending: Cassia (4800), Bjorn (2400), Alice (1200), Dorian (80). LIMIT 2 takes the first two — Cassia and Bjorn.

questions.questionHtml: Which clause goes before which? Pick the only valid ordering.
options: SELECT → FROM → WHERE → ORDER BY → LIMIT
SELECT → WHERE → FROM → ORDER BY → LIMIT
SELECT → FROM → ORDER BY → WHERE → LIMIT
SELECT → FROM → LIMIT → WHERE → ORDER BY
questions.correctAnswer: SELECT → FROM → WHERE → ORDER BY → LIMIT
questions.explanationHtml: This is fixed by the SQL grammar. The engine evaluates them in a different order (FROM and WHERE happen before SELECT internally), but you must write them in this sequence or the parser rejects the query.

questions.questionHtml:
A junior writes the following query:

SELECT name FROM apprentices LIMIT 3;

Why is this almost always a bug, even though it runs without error?
options: There is no ORDER BY, so 'three rows' could be any three rows the engine happens to return — not the top three or the first three by any meaningful sense
LIMIT 3 always returns the same three rows in every engine, so the query is trivially correct
SELECT name without WHERE is a syntax error
LIMIT must always be the last word in the query, including after the semicolon
questions.correctAnswer: There is no ORDER BY, so 'three rows' could be any three rows the engine happens to return — not the top three or the first three by any meaningful sense
questions.explanationHtml: The relational model says rows are an unordered set. Without ORDER BY, "the first three" has no defined meaning — different engines, different storage orders, even different query plans, can return different rows. This is the most common SQL bug for newcomers: writing LIMIT without ORDER BY and assuming a stable result.
